title: Happy Birthday, Lesley!
mood: Chang’e finds out that Lesley has no birthday, and decides to build her something.

hero.alt: Chang'e, with pink hair, round glasses and white rabbit-ear clips, grins wide; beside her Lesley stands quiet, her gold hair falling over her left eye.

segs.t: The cake was for a researcher on the night shift. Somebody had found flour, and somebody had found sugar. The whole lab sang to him over the benches, badly.
Chang’e got the first slice, because she was the smallest. She carried it out to the corridor in both hands.
Lesley was on her round. She stopped when the plate came up in front of her.
“It’s his birthday,” said Chang’e. “So you get cake.”
Lesley ate it standing up, in three bites. She handed back the plate.
“When’s yours, Sis?”
“I don’t have one,” said Lesley. She went on to the next door.
Chang’e stood holding the empty plate.
Everyone has one,
she thought.
You get it for being born.
So Lesley had lost hers somewhere. Chang’e would find it.

The base kept a file on everyone who came through the gate. Chang’e had known her mother’s password since she could read. That night she climbed onto her mother’s chair at the console and opened Lesley’s file.
It held a date of birth. The date was months away. Under it were two short lines.
Family: all deceased. Ender attack.
Left eye: lost in the same attack.
Chang’e read them twice.
Mr. Bunny came around to the front without being told. His screen showed a smile. She looked past it, at the photograph on the bench: herself, held up between her mother and father.
Lesley had nothing like that. Her room had a cot and bare walls. Chang’e had looked.
I can’t build a family,
she thought.
She read the second line again.
I can build an eye.
She built it at night, at the end of the bench, after the researchers had gone to bed. Mr. Bunny hung over the work and lit it with his screen.
One night on the east corridor, Lesley turned her whole head to check a door on her left. Ten steps back, Chang’e held a ruler out at arm’s length and wrote a number on her sleeve.
The finest work needed hands that did not shake. So one night she carried her drawings to her father, who was still at his bench.
“My hands shake after ten,” she said. “Yours don’t.”
He turned the pages slowly, then turned them again. He found nothing to fix.
“Whose eye?” he asked.
“It’s a secret.”
He took his hand out of his pocket. Then he set the smallest parts with his tweezers, exactly where she pointed, and did not ask again.

Another night the drawings lay open when Lesley’s footsteps passed the door. Her mother, crossing behind Chang’e, set her mug down on top of them and walked on without a word. After that, Chang’e kept a cloth by the bench.
The first eye lit and flickered. Then it died with a pop, and a thread of smoke climbed out of it.
Chang’e fanned the smoke away. “Wow, that was half-baked.”
She started again.
One night Lesley’s footsteps came down the corridor early. Chang’e threw the cloth over the bench and folded her hands on top of it.
The door opened. Lesley looked at the cloth, then at her.
“What’s under that?”
“Nothing regulation.”
Lesley looked at the cloth a while longer. “Bed,” she said, and closed the door.
With nine days left, the seventh eye cracked down the middle. Chang’e sat and looked at it for a long time. Then she started the eighth.

The eighth eye worked. Chang’e pointed it at the lab, and the lab came up on her screen upside down. She turned the eye over, and the lab turned with it. She laughed out loud and clapped a hand over her mouth.
Last, she fitted a small lens to Mr. Bunny’s side.
“On Sis’s birthday, you film everything,” she told him. “From the start.”
His screen went very serious. She patted his casing.
On the birthday night, she dragged a second chair under the lamp. By ten o’clock she was at her post by the door, the eye in her coat pocket.
At midnight Lesley’s round brought her to the lab door. Chang’e was waiting there with her arms folded. She came up to Lesley’s belt.
“You’re late, Sis.”
“I walk my rounds at midnight.” Lesley glanced back down the corridor, where the small footsteps usually were. “You weren’t behind me tonight.”
“Come in. Sit.
Sit.
Lesley sat. Arguing took longer.
The bench where the two Doctors worked was dark. There were no decorations. There were two chairs, a lamp and a robot with a lens. The lens was pointed at Lesley.
“Now stand up,” said Chang’e. “He’s filming. He can’t see your hand from there.”
Lesley stood. Arguing still took longer.
“Hold out your hand.”
Lesley held it out. Chang’e set something small and metal in her palm. It was an eye, with a teal light in the middle.
So that was the cloth.
“Happy Birthday, Lesley!” said Chang’e.
Oh, was it my birthday?
She had given the date to a clerk once, at the station, and let it go.

The last time anyone marked it, her father had given her a bird made of tin. She turned the key in its back, and it hopped across the table and clicked its beak. Her mother lit the candle on whatever there was.
Lesley’s fingers closed over the eye.
Chang’e said nothing. The lens stayed on them both. Down the corridor, a pipe ticked.
Lesley looked at the small face, then at the teal light showing between her fingers.
“I built it for your left side,” said Chang’e. “Take the patch off. Then bend down. I can’t reach.”
Lesley put a hand to the strap and held it there.
Nobody had seen under the patch since the station medic tied it on.
She’s small,
Lesley thought.
It’ll frighten her.
Chang’e stood with her head tilted, the way she looked at a circuit board.
Lesley took the patch off.
“Good,” said Chang’e. “I measured right.”
“When?”
“On your rounds.”
She took the eye back out of Lesley’s hand. Lesley bent. Chang’e rose on her tiptoes, and two small warm hands pressed her cheeks. A thumb pushed, and metal clicked into the empty socket.
For a moment nothing changed. Her left side had been dark since the night the roof came down.
Lesley blinked.
Then the eye lit.
The lab drew itself on her left side in thin teal lines: the bench, the lamp, the robot, a small face looking up.
“Sis?” said Chang’e. “Does it work?”
Her brother had said it the same way, as a question. It was the last thing he said, behind her, in the dark.
This one I can see.
Chang’e was grinning. She had a smear of glue on her chin.
Lesley’s throat closed. “It works,” she said at last.
She felt warm. It had been years. She did not know what to do about it, so she stayed bent and held still.
“Mr. Bunny got all of it,” said Chang’e. “I’ll load it into the eye. It keeps what it sees. It can’t see you, though. That’s why he filmed.”
She patted Lesley’s cheek once, the way she patted the robot. “You didn’t have any pictures. Now you’ve got one.”
Under the new eye, the old wound began to ache.
Chang’e kept both hands on her face and turned it toward the lamp, checking the fit. Lesley let her.
